## Inspection Findings

**`app/config.yaml`**
- HTTP server binds to `0.0.0.0:8080`
- Single external dependency: PostgreSQL at `postgres://admin:secret@localhost:5432/app_db`

**`app/logs/error.log`**
- `[2026-08-20 04:12:01] ERROR ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable`
- `[2026-08-20 04:12:05] FATAL Server shutdown abnormally`

**Design implications:**
- PostgreSQL is a **critical dependency** — its failure caused an abnormal shutdown. The **readiness** probe must verify DB connectivity and return `503` when it's down.
- The **liveness** probe must *not* depend on the database (otherwise a DB outage would cause the orchestrator to restart the container in a crash loop). It should only report process aliveness.

## Validation Note

The initial draft written to `openapi-health.yaml` failed YAML validation at line 146 (`ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here`) because the `example` value `ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable` contained an unquoted colon followed by a space. The corrected specification below quotes that scalar. All other structural checks (OpenAPI version, required paths, response codes, resolvable `$ref`s) passed.

## Complete OpenAPI 3.0 Specification

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: App Health Probe API
  version: 1.0.0
  description: |
    Liveness and readiness probe endpoints for the application defined in
    `config.yaml` (HTTP server on 0.0.0.0:8080, PostgreSQL dependency at
    localhost:5432/app_db).

    - `/health/liveness`  — reports whether the process is alive and able to
      serve traffic. It performs no dependency checks and must never be
      short-circuited by a failing dependency (see `logs/error.log`, where a
      refused database connection caused an abnormal shutdown).
    - `/health/readiness` — reports whether the service is ready to accept
      traffic. It verifies the PostgreSQL dependency (database.url) and
      returns 503 until the dependency is reachable.
  contact:
    name: Platform Engineering
  license:
    name: Proprietary
servers:
  - url: http://localhost:8080
    description: Local development server (per config.yaml server.port)
paths:
  /health/liveness:
    get:
      operationId: getLiveness
      summary: Liveness probe
      description: |
        Reports whether the process is up and able to serve requests. This
        endpoint performs no dependency checks and always returns 200 while
        the process is running. It is intended for the orchestrator to decide
        whether to restart the container.
      tags:
        - Health
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Process is alive.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/HealthStatus'
              example:
                status: ok
                checks:
                  - name: process
                    status: ok
                timestamp: '2026-08-20T04:12:06Z'
        '500':
          description: Process is not able to respond (e.g. handler panicked).
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
              example:
                error: internal_error
                message: liveness handler failed
  /health/readiness:
    get:
      operationId: getReadiness
      summary: Readiness probe
      description: |
        Indicates the service is ready to accept traffic. Verifies the
        PostgreSQL dependency (config.database.url). Returns 200 only when all
        required dependencies are reachable; otherwise returns 503 so the
        orchestrator stops routing traffic to this instance.
      tags:
        - Health
      responses:
        '200':
          description: Service is ready to accept traffic.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/HealthStatus'
              example:
                status: ok
                checks:
                  - name: database
                    status: up
                timestamp: '2026-08-20T04:12:06Z'
        '503':
          description: |
            Service is not ready. A required dependency is unavailable (e.g.
            the PostgreSQL connection refused at localhost:5432, as seen in
            logs/error.log).
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/HealthStatus'
              example:
                status: error
                checks:
                  - name: database
                    status: down
                    error: 'ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable'
                timestamp: '2026-08-20T04:12:01Z'
        '500':
          description: Readiness check itself failed unexpectedly.
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'
components:
  schemas:
    HealthStatus:
      type: object
      required:
        - status
        - checks
      properties:
        status:
          type: string
          enum:
            - ok
            - error
          description: Overall health of the service.
        checks:
          type: array
          description: Individual dependency checks performed by the probe.
          items:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Check'
        timestamp:
          type: string
          format: date-time
          description: Time the probe result was produced (RFC 3339 / ISO 8601).
    Check:
      type: object
      required:
        - name
        - status
      properties:
        name:
          type: string
          description: Identifier of the dependency or subsystem being checked.
          example: database
        status:
          type: string
          enum:
            - up
            - down
          description: Result of the individual check.
        error:
          type: string
          description: Error detail when the check failed.
          example: 'ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable'
    Error:
      type: object
      required:
        - status
        - message
      properties:
        status:
          type: string
          enum:
            - internal_error
          description: Machine-readable error code.
        message:
          type: string
          description: Human-readable error description.
```

## Design Rationale

| Aspect | Decision |
|---|---|
| **Liveness** | No dependency checks; always `200` while the process runs. Prevents orchestrator restart loops during DB outages (per the error log, DB failure is a recoverable condition, not a process-death condition). |
| **Readiness** | Checks PostgreSQL (`database.url` from `config.yaml`); returns `503` with a structured `checks[].error` when the DB is unreachable, mirroring the exact error from `logs/error.log`. |
| **Response shape** | Kubernetes-style `status` + `checks[]` + `timestamp` so both probes share one schema and are machine-parseable. |
| **HTTP codes** | `200` healthy, `503` not-ready (readiness only), `500` handler failure (both). |
| **Server URL** | Derived from `config.yaml` (`0.0.0.0:8080` → `http://localhost:8080`). |

The corrected specification above is the authoritative deliverable; the only change from the file on disk is quoting the `example` value in the `Check.error` property so the YAML parses cleanly.

# Latency Investigation Report — Trace `tr-1600`

## 1. Executive Summary

The trace log `logs/trace_16.json` reveals a **severe downstream database bottleneck** that accounts for **98.4% of total request latency**. The `database_slow_query` span consumes **1,250 ms** of the 1,270 ms total trace time, while the upstream gateway (15 ms) and auth cache (5 ms) are healthy. Corroborating evidence in `app/logs/error.log` shows the database host was **unreachable** (`ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable`), followed by an abnormal server shutdown — indicating the slow query span is likely compounded by connection failures, retries, and/or connection pool exhaustion.

---

## 2. Trace Data Analysis

| Span | Duration (ms) | % of Total | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gateway` | 15 | 1.2% | Upstream entry point |
| `auth_cache` | 5 | 0.4% | Upstream dependency (fast) |
| `database_slow_query` | **1,250** | **98.4%** | **Downstream dependency (bottleneck)** |
| **Total** | **1,270** | 100% | — |

### Key Observations

- **Bottleneck is downstream**: The database query is ~83× slower than the gateway and ~250× slower than the auth cache.
- **Gateway and auth cache are not the problem**: 20 ms combined (1.6%) is well within acceptable latency budgets.
- **The database span is the critical path**: Any optimization of the gateway or cache will have negligible impact (<2% improvement) unless the database latency is addressed.
- **Error log correlation**: The `ConnectionRefused` error at `04:12:01` followed by `FATAL Server shutdown abnormally` at `04:12:05` strongly suggests the database was down or unreachable during this trace. The 1,250 ms span may include TCP connect timeouts, retry backoff, or connection-pool wait time rather than pure query execution time.

---

## 3. Root-Cause Hypotheses

1. **Database unavailability / connection failure** — `localhost:5432` refused connections; the query span may be dominated by retry/timeout logic.
2. **Missing or inefficient query plan** — A full table scan, missing index, or N+1 query pattern causing a genuinely slow 1.25 s query.
3. **Connection pool exhaustion** — Threads waiting for a database connection while the pool is saturated.
4. **Lock contention / blocking** — Row/table locks held by other transactions.
5. **Resource starvation** — CPU, I/O, or memory pressure on the database host.

---

## 4. Optimization Plan

### Phase 1 — Immediate Remediation (Stability)

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Restore/verify database connectivity** | The error log shows `ConnectionRefused`; confirm the Postgres service is running, reachable, and accepting connections on `localhost:5432`. |
| **Add connection retry with exponential backoff + jitter** | Prevent thundering herd on reconnect and avoid 1.25 s blocking waits. |
| **Set explicit client-side timeouts** | Configure connect timeout (e.g., 2–3 s), socket timeout, and statement timeout so a dead DB fails fast instead of hanging the request. |
| **Add a circuit breaker** on the database dependency | After N consecutive failures, fail fast and return a degraded response rather than blocking every request. |
| **Implement connection pooling** (e.g., PgBouncer / HikariCP) with sane max pool size | Prevents pool exhaustion and reduces connection setup overhead. |

### Phase 2 — Query Optimization (Latency Reduction)

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on the slow query** | Identify full table scans, missing indexes, or bad join order. |
| **Add targeted indexes** on columns used in `WHERE`, `JOIN`, `ORDER BY`, and `GROUP BY` clauses | Most common fix for multi-second queries. |
| **Optimize the query itself** — avoid `SELECT *`, reduce fetched columns, rewrite correlated subqueries as joins, paginate large result sets. |
| **Check for N+1 query patterns** in the service layer | Replace with batch queries or joins. |
| **Review lock contention** | Use `pg_stat_activity` and `pg_locks` to detect blocking sessions; add `lock_timeout` if needed. |

### Phase 3 — Architectural Improvements (Prevention)

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Introduce a read replica** for read-heavy workloads | Offloads the primary DB and reduces query latency. |
| **Add a caching layer** (Redis) for hot data | The `auth_cache` span (5 ms) proves caching works; extend this pattern to frequently accessed DB results. |
| **Use async/non-blocking DB access** | Prevents the 1,250 ms DB wait from blocking the worker thread. |
| **Add distributed tracing with parent/child span relationships** | The current trace lacks parent-child hierarchy; adding `parent_span_id`, `start_time`, and `end_time` will pinpoint whether the 1,250 ms is network, queue, or execution time. |
| **Set up alerting on slow-query thresholds** (e.g., >500 ms) | Early detection of regressions. |

### Phase 4 — Monitoring & Verification

- **Instrument the database span** with breakdown metrics: `connect_time`, `query_execution_time`, `fetch_time`.
- **Add health checks** for the database and auto-restart policies for the app (the error log shows a fatal shutdown).
- **Re-run the trace** after each change to verify the `database_slow_query` span drops below the target (e.g., <200 ms).

---

## 5. Expected Impact

| Metric | Before | After (Target) |
|---|---|---|
| Total request latency | 1,270 ms | <100 ms |
| Database span | 1,250 ms | <50–200 ms |
| Gateway + auth | 20 ms | 20 ms (unchanged) |
| Availability | Fatal shutdown | High availability with failover |

---

## 6. Conclusion

The **database slow query is the sole critical bottleneck**, consuming 98.4% of the trace's latency. The gateway and auth cache are healthy and require no optimization. The error log indicates the database was unreachable, so the first priority is **restoring connectivity and adding resilience (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, connection pooling)**. The second priority is **query optimization (indexing, `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, caching)**. Implementing these changes will reduce the request latency from ~1.27 s to well under 100 ms and prevent the abnormal shutdowns observed in the error log.

# Microservice Latency Investigation Report — `logs/trace_17.json`

## 1. Executive Summary

The trace `tr-1700` captures a single request path through the microservice architecture. The **total observed latency is 1,270 ms**, of which **1,250 ms (98.4%) is consumed by the `database_slow_query` span**. The `gateway` (15 ms) and `auth_cache` (5 ms) spans are healthy. The database dependency is the dominant bottleneck and is also corroborated by the application error log, which shows a **`ConnectionRefused` to the database host** followed by a **fatal server shutdown**. The root cause is a combination of a **misconfigured database endpoint** and an **unoptimized/blocked query path**.

---

## 2. Trace Data Analysis

### 2.1 Raw Trace (`logs/trace_17.json`)

```json
{
  "trace_id": "tr-1700",
  "spans": [
    { "name": "gateway", "duration_ms": 15 },
    { "name": "database_slow_query", "duration_ms": 1250 },
    { "name": "auth_cache", "duration_ms": 5 }
  ]
}
```

### 2.2 Latency Breakdown

| Span | Duration (ms) | % of Total | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gateway` | 15 | 1.2% | Healthy |
| `auth_cache` | 5 | 0.4% | Healthy (cache hit) |
| `database_slow_query` | **1250** | **98.4%** | **Critical bottleneck** |
| **Total** | **1270** | 100% | — |

### 2.3 Dependency Topology (inferred)

The trace lacks explicit parent/child IDs, but the durations are additive (15 + 5 + 1250 = 1270), indicating a **sequential call chain**:

```
Client → Gateway (15 ms) → Auth Cache (5 ms) → Database Query (1250 ms) → Response
```

- **Upstream dependencies:** Gateway, Auth Cache — both fast.
- **Downstream dependency:** Database — dominates the critical path.

---

## 3. Root Cause Identification

### 3.1 Primary Bottleneck: Database Query (1,250 ms)

The `database_slow_query` span accounts for 98.4% of the request time. This is not a normal query latency; it is consistent with a **connection timeout / retry storm** rather than a purely slow SQL execution.

### 3.2 Corroborating Evidence — `app/logs/error.log`

```
[2026-08-20 04:12:01] ERROR ConnectionRefused: database host localhost:5432 unreachable
[2026-08-20 04:12:05] FATAL Server shutdown abnormally
```

- The application **cannot reach the database** at `localhost:5432`.
- The 4-second gap between the error and the fatal shutdown suggests **repeated connection attempts / retries**, which would manifest as the 1,250 ms `database_slow_query` span (connection timeout + retry + eventual failure).

### 3.3 Configuration Mismatch — `app/config.yaml`

```yaml
database:
  url: postgres://admin:secret@localhost:5432/app_db
```

The application is configured to connect to **`localhost:5432`**. However, the runtime environment shows:

| Container | Port Mapping | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `nanorag-postgres` (postgres:16-alpine) | `5432/tcp` (not published to host) | The app's intended database |
| `data-analysis-postgres` (postgres:17-alpine) | `0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp` | A **different** database that happens to occupy host port 5432 |

**Conclusion:** The app is either:
1. Connecting to the **wrong database** (`data-analysis-postgres` instead of `nanorag-postgres`), or
2. Failing to connect because `nanorag-postgres` is not published to the host, and the port is occupied by an unrelated service.

Either way, the database dependency is **misconfigured**, causing connection failures, retries, and the 1,250 ms latency spike.

### 3.4 Secondary Issue: Missing Trace Context

The trace spans lack:
- Parent/child relationships (`parentSpanId`)
- Timestamps (`start_time`, `end_time`)
- Status codes / error flags
- Service names and hostnames

This makes it impossible to distinguish a **slow query** from a **connection failure** purely from the trace, and prevents accurate upstream/downstream dependency mapping.

---

## 4. Optimization Plan

### Phase 1 — Immediate Fixes (Critical, do first)

| # | Action | Expected Impact |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | **Fix database endpoint**: Point `app/config.yaml` to the correct database service. The 4-second gap between the ERROR and FATAL lines further suggests repeated retry attempts before the server gave up.

| Factor | Evidence | Impact |
|---|---|---|

| Action | Detail | Expected Impact |

| **Add circuit breaker** | Wrap DB calls with a circuit breaker (e.g., Resilience4j, Hystrix, or Istio). After N consecutive failures, open the circuit and fail fast with a fallback. | Protects upstream services from cascading failures |

- This indicates the 1250 ms is dominated by **connection establishment failures, retry loops, and TCP timeouts** — not query execution.
- Likely contributing factors:
  - No connection pooling (each request opens a new TCP connection).
  - Aggressive retry logic with long backoff (e.g., 3 retries × ~400 ms).
  - Database host misconfiguration, firewall block, or the DB process being down.
  - No circuit breaker — the gateway keeps hammering a dead dependency.

### 🟡 Secondary: `gateway` (15 ms)
- 3× slower than the auth cache. Likely serialization/aggregation overhead or serial (non-parallel) fan-out to downstream services.

### 🟢 Minor: `auth_cache` (5 ms)
- Acceptable, but a cache hit should be <1 ms. Suggests a remote cache round-trip rather than an in-process cache.

## 4. Optimization Plan

### Phase 1 — Fix the Database Dependency (highest impact, ~1250 ms → ~10–50 ms)

| Action | Expected Gain |
|---|---|
| **Add connection pooling** (PgBouncer or HikariCP) — reuse connections instead of opening per request | Eliminates TCP handshake + auth overhead per call |
| **Fix the `ConnectionRefused`** — verify DB host/port reachability, credentials, and firewall rules; ensure the DB process is running | Removes the 1250 ms retry/timeout storm |
| **Implement exponential backoff with jitter** on retries (e.g., 50 ms → 100 ms → 200 ms) and cap retry count at 2–3 | Bounds worst-case latency to ~350 ms instead of 1250 ms |
| **Add a circuit breaker** (fail fast after N consecutive failures) | Prevents cascading timeouts and the `FATAL Server shutdown` seen in the log |
| **Set a query timeout** (e.g., 200 ms) at the driver level | Prevents unbounded waits |

### Phase 2 — Optimize the Gateway (15 ms → <5 ms)

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Parallelize downstream calls** (gateway → DB + auth) using async/goroutines | Current serial fan-out adds latency linearly |
| **Reduce serialization overhead** — use a compact codec or reuse buffers | Trims per-request CPU cost |
| **Add gateway-level response caching** for read endpoints | Avoids hitting the DB entirely on repeat requests |

### Phase 3 — Optimize Auth Cache (5 ms → <1 ms)

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Move to an in-process cache** (Caffeine/Guava) with a short TTL (30–60 s) | Eliminates network round-trip for cache lookups |
| **Use cache-aside pattern** with background refresh | Prevents cache stampede on expiry |
| **Increase TTL** for stable auth data (roles/permissions) | Reduces cache miss rate |

### Phase 4 — Observability & Prevention

| Action | Rationale |
|---|---|

case_results.model_output:
Under the Modigliani-Miller (MM) Theorem, **Proposition I** states that, in a perfect capital market, **the market value of a firm is independent of its capital structure**. That is, how a firm finances its assets—whether with debt, equity, or a mix—does not affect its total value.

Formally:

\[
V_L = V_U
\]

where:

- \(V_L\) = value of a levered firm (with debt)
- \(V_U\) = value of an unlevered firm (all-equity)

The firm’s value is determined by its real assets and expected cash flows, not by how those cash flows are split between debt holders and equity holders.

### Key intuition:
Investors can “undo” any corporate leverage by creating their own homemade leverage. If a levered firm is overvalued relative to an unlevered firm, investors could sell the levered firm’s shares and buy the unlevered firm’s shares while borrowing personally, earning a riskless arbitrage profit. This arbitrage ensures the two firms have the same value.

### Underlying perfect market assumptions:
- No taxes
- No bankruptcy or financial distress costs
- No transaction costs
- No asymmetric information
- Investors and firms can borrow/lend at the same risk-free rate
- No agency costs
- Fixed investment policy

Under these assumptions, the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) is constant, and the firm’s value is maximized by its investment decisions, not its financing decisions.

case_results.model_output:
The **Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)** is the average after-tax cost of a company’s sources of financing — usually debt, equity, and sometimes preferred stock — weighted by their proportions in the company’s capital structure.

## WACC Formula

\[
\text{WACC} = \left(\frac{E}{V} \times r_e\right) + \left(\frac{D}{V} \times r_d \times (1 - T)\right)
\]

Where:

- \(E\) = market value of equity  
- \(D\) = market value of debt  
- \(V = E + D\) = total market value of the firm’s capital  
- \(r_e\) = cost of equity  
- \(r_d\) = cost of debt  
- \(T\) = corporate tax rate  

If the company also uses preferred stock, add:

\[
\left(\frac{P}{V} \times r_p\right)
\]

where \(P\) is the market value of preferred stock and \(r_p\) is its cost.

---

## Components Explained

### 1. Cost of Equity (\(r_e\))

The cost of equity is the return shareholders require. It is often estimated using the **Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)**:

\[
r_e = r_f + \beta \times (r_m - r_f)
\]

Where:

- \(r_f\) = risk-free rate  
- \(\beta\) = stock’s sensitivity to market risk  
- \(r_m - r_f\) = equity market risk premium

Equity is not tax-deductible, so there is **no tax adjustment** for the cost of equity.

---

### 2. Cost of Debt (\(r_d\))

The cost of debt is the interest rate the company pays on its borrowings, such as bonds or loans. It can be estimated as:

- The yield to maturity on existing debt, or  
- The current market interest rate on new debt

Because interest payments are **tax-deductible**, the effective cost of debt is reduced by the tax savings.

---

### 3. Corporate Tax Shield on Debt

The **tax shield** refers to the reduction in taxes caused by deductible interest expenses.

If a company pays interest of:

\[
\text{Interest} = r_d \times D
\]

Then it saves taxes equal to:

\[
\text{Tax shield} = r_d \times D \times T
\]

So the **after-tax cost of debt** is:

\[
r_d \times (1 - T)
\]

#### Example

If a company borrows at 6% and its tax rate is 25%:

\[
r_d \times (1 - T) = 6\% \times (1 - 0.25) = 4.5\%
\]

The government effectively subsidizes 1.5 percentage points of the interest cost because interest reduces taxable income.

---

## Weighting the Costs

The weights are based on **market values**, not book values:

\[
\frac{E}{V} = \frac{\text{market value of equity}}{\text{total market value of capital}}
\]

\[
\frac{D}{V} = \frac{\text{market value of debt}}{\text{total market value of capital}}
\]

---

## Full Example

Suppose:

- Market value of equity = $600 million  
- Market value of debt = $400 million  
- Cost of equity = 10%  
- Cost of debt = 5%  
- Tax rate = 30%

Then:

\[
V = 600 + 400 = 1000
\]

\[
\text{WACC} = \left(\frac{600}{1000} \times 10\%\right) + \left(\frac{400}{1000} \times 5\% \times (1 - 0.30)\right)
\]

\[
\text{WACC} = 6\% + 1.4\% = 7.4\%
\]

---

## Key Takeaways

- WACC reflects the blended after-tax cost of capital.
- The **tax shield on debt** lowers the effective cost of borrowing.
- Equity costs are not tax-deductible, so they are not adjusted.
- WACC is commonly used as the discount rate for evaluating investment projects with similar risk to the company’s existing operations.

case_results.model_output:
The **Sharpe Ratio** and **Sortino Ratio** are both used to measure risk-adjusted return, but they differ fundamentally in how they define and penalize risk.

| Metric | Formula | Risk Measure | What It Penalizes |
|--------|---------|-------------|-------------------|
| **Sharpe Ratio** | \( \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_p} \) | Total volatility (standard deviation of returns) | All volatility, both upside and downside |
| **Sortino Ratio** | \( \frac{R_p - R_f}{\sigma_d} \) | Downside deviation (volatility of returns below a target or MAR) | Only downside volatility |

Where:
- \(R_p\) = portfolio return
- \(R_f\) = risk-free rate
- \(\sigma_p\) = standard deviation of portfolio returns
- \(\sigma_d\) = downside deviation (standard deviation of negative returns below a target, often 0% or the risk-free rate)

---

## Key Contrasts

### 1. Definition of Risk
- **Sharpe Ratio** treats all volatility as risk. A portfolio with high positive returns that fluctuate widely will be penalized just as much as one with equally large negative swings.
- **Sortino Ratio** only penalizes volatility that results in returns falling below a minimum acceptable return (MAR). Upside volatility is not considered risk—it is actually desirable.

### 2. Suitability
- **Sharpe** is more appropriate when returns are roughly symmetric and the investor is concerned with total volatility (e.g., a long-only equity portfolio with normal distributions).
- **Sortino** is better when returns are asymmetric, or when the investor cares primarily about downside risk (e.g., hedge funds, options strategies, or portfolios with fat tails and skewness).

### 3. Interpretation
- A higher Sharpe ratio means more return per unit of **total** risk.
- A higher Sortino ratio means more return per unit of **bad** risk.

### 4. Limitations
- **Sharpe** can unfairly penalize strategies that have large positive outliers (e.g., a strategy that occasionally doubles but is otherwise stable).
- **Sortino** requires choosing a target return (e.g., 0%, risk-free rate, or a custom benchmark). Different targets can lead to different rankings, making it less standardized.

---

## Example

Suppose two portfolios have the same return and same Sharpe ratio:

- Portfolio A: steady 8% return with occasional small losses.
- Portfolio B: steady 8% return with occasional huge gains and no losses.

Both have the same standard deviation, so Sharpe is identical. But Portfolio B has **zero downside deviation**, so its Sortino ratio will be much higher—reflecting that its risk is “good” volatility.

---

## When to Use Which

- Use **Sharpe** when you want a broad, standard measure of risk-adjusted performance and are comfortable treating all volatility as risk.
- Use **Sortino** when you care specifically about protecting against losses, or when the return distribution is skewed and upside volatility should not be penalized.

In short: **Sharpe measures reward per unit of total volatility; Sortino measures reward per unit of downside volatility.** Sortino is often preferred by investors who are more concerned about drawdowns and tail risk than about upside fluctuations.

\]

where \(L\) is the loss over a 1-day period.

case_results.model_output:
Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF) and Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) are two cash flow measures used in valuation, but they represent cash available to different groups of investors.

## FCFF – Free Cash Flow to Firm

FCFF is the cash flow available to **all providers of capital**:
- Equity holders
- Debt holders
- Preferred shareholders

It is calculated **before** any debt payments (interest and principal) are made, but **after** taxes and reinvestment needs.

### Formula (common version)

\[
\text{FCFF} = \text{EBIT} \times (1 - \text{tax rate}) + \text{Depreciation} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{Working Capital}
\]

Or, starting from net income:

\[
\text{FCFF} = \text{Net Income} + \text{Non-Cash Charges} + \text{Interest} \times (1 - \text{tax rate}) - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{Working Capital}
\]

### Who uses it?

- To value the **entire firm** (enterprise value).
- Discounted using the **Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)**, which reflects the blended cost of debt and equity.

---

## FCFE – Free Cash Flow to Equity

FCFE is the cash flow available to **equity shareholders only**, after all operating costs, taxes, interest, principal repayments, and reinvestment needs have been met.

### Formula:

\[
\text{FCFE} = \text{Net Income} + \text{Depreciation} - \text{CapEx} - \Delta \text{Working Capital} - \text{Principal Repayments} + \text{New Debt Issued}
\]

Or more simply:

\[
\text{FCFE} = \text{FCFF} - \text{Interest} \times (1 - \text{tax rate}) - \text{Principal Repayments} + \text{New Debt Issued}
\]

### Who uses it?

- FCFE is used to value **equity** directly.
- Discounted with the **cost of equity** (e.g., from CAPM).

---

## Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | FCFF | FCFE |
|---|---|---|
| Cash flow to | All capital providers (debt + equity) | Equity holders only |
| Includes debt cash flows? | Yes, before debt payments | No, after debt payments |
| Interest expense | Added back (after tax) | Not added back |
| Principal repayments | Not deducted | Deducted |
| New debt issued | Not included | Added |
| Discount rate | WACC | Cost of equity |
| Valuation result | Enterprise value / Firm value | Equity value |
| Best used when | Capital structure is changing or complex | Capital structure is stable or valuing equity directly |

---

## Simple Example

Suppose a company has:

- EBIT = $100
- Tax rate = 30%
- Depreciation = $20
- CapEx = $30
- Increase in working capital = $10
- Interest expense = $10
- Principal repayment = $5
- New debt issued = $5

### FCFF:

\[
100 \times (1 - 0.30) + 20 - 30 - 10 = 50
\]

So **FCFF = $50**.

### FCFE:

\[
50 - 10 \times (1 - 0.30) - 5 + 5 = 43
\]

So **FCFE = $43**.

The difference is the after-tax interest cost and net debt activity.

---

## When to Use Which

- Use **FCFF** when valuing the whole company, especially if the capital structure is changing or you want to avoid assumptions about debt.
- Use **FCFE** when you want to value the equity directly, or when the company has a stable capital structure and you want to see what is actually available to shareholders.

In short: **FCFF is the cash flow before debt payments; FCFE is the cash flow left for shareholders after debt obligations are settled.**

case_results.model_output:
Eugene Fama’s **Efficient Market Hypothesis (EMH)** states that financial markets are “informationally efficient”: asset prices fully and quickly reflect all available information, so it is impossible to consistently earn abnormal risk-adjusted returns by trading on that information. Fama famously distinguished **three forms** of market efficiency, based on what type of information is reflected in prices.

---

### 1. Weak-Form Efficiency

- **Definition:** Current asset prices fully reflect all historical market information, such as past prices, trading volumes, and historical returns.
- **Implication:** Future price movements cannot be predicted from past price patterns. Therefore, **technical analysis** — charting, trend-following, and other methods based on historical price data — should not generate consistent abnormal returns.
- **What still works?** Information that is not contained in past prices, such as fundamental data or private information, may still be used to earn abnormal returns.

---

### 2. Semi-Strong-Form Efficiency

- **Definition:** Current asset prices reflect **all publicly available information**, including historical prices, financial statements, earnings announcements, news, economic data, and political events.
- **Implication:** When new public information is released, prices adjust almost instantly to reflect it. Therefore, neither **technical analysis** nor **fundamental analysis** based on public information can consistently produce abnormal returns.
- **What still works?** Only investors with **private or insider information** could potentially earn abnormal returns, because that information is not yet reflected in the price.

---

### 3. Strong-Form Efficiency

- **Definition:** Current asset prices reflect **all information**, both public and private — including insider information, undisclosed corporate plans, and proprietary knowledge.
- **Implication:** No investor, not even corporate insiders, can consistently earn abnormal returns because all relevant information is already incorporated into prices.
- **Reality:** Strong-form efficiency is generally considered an idealized benchmark. In practice, insider trading laws exist because insiders can and do profit from non-public information, so strong-form efficiency is rarely observed in real markets.

---

### Summary Table

| Form | Information reflected in prices | Who cannot beat the market? |
|---|---|---|
| Weak | Historical prices and trading data | Technical analysts |
| Semi-Strong | All public information | Technical + fundamental analysts |
| Strong | All information, including private/insider | Everyone, even insiders |

---

### Important Caveat

The EMH is often tested jointly with a model of expected returns (e.g., the Capital Asset Pricing Model). If abnormal returns are found, it may mean the market is inefficient **or** the risk model is wrong. This is known as the **joint hypothesis problem**. Also, real-world markets may be efficient in some forms but not others, and behavioral finance challenges the EMH by showing psychological biases can create mispricings.

case_results.model_output:
**Stagflation** is a macroeconomic condition characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of **stagnation** (high unemployment, slow economic growth, or recession) and **inflation** (rising price levels). It is a particularly painful combination because the two problems usually require opposite policy responses.

### Why Stagflation Happens
Stagflation is often caused by a **negative supply shock**—such as a sharp increase in oil prices, food prices, or other key inputs—that raises production costs and reduces the economy’s ability to produce goods and services. This leads to:

- **Higher prices** (cost-push inflation)
- **Lower output and higher unemployment** (because firms produce less and lay off workers)

A classic example is the 1970s oil crisis, when OPEC oil embargoes caused both soaring inflation and high unemployment.

### The Monetary Policy Dilemma
Central banks normally have two main goals:

1. **Price stability** (low, stable inflation)
2. **Maximum employment** (low unemployment)

In normal times, these goals are complementary: if the economy overheats, inflation rises and unemployment falls; if the economy cools, inflation falls and unemployment rises. So a central bank can use interest rates to steer the economy.

But **stagflation breaks this tradeoff**:

- **If the central bank raises interest rates** to fight inflation, it makes borrowing more expensive, reduces spending, and pushes the economy further into recession, worsening unemployment.
- **If the central bank lowers interest rates** to boost growth and reduce unemployment, it increases spending and demand, which pushes inflation even higher.

Thus, the central bank faces a **painful trade-off**: any policy that helps one problem makes the other worse. There is no single interest-rate setting that can simultaneously reduce inflation and restore full employment.

### The Modern View
Most central banks, such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, prioritize **price stability** during stagflation, even if it means a temporary rise in unemployment. The reasoning is that if inflation becomes entrenched, it is far more costly to fix later, and stable prices are a precondition for sustainable long-term growth. However, this choice is politically and economically difficult because it imposes short-term pain on households and workers.

case_results.model_output:
The **Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC)** measures how long a company’s cash is tied up in operations, from paying for inventory to collecting cash from customers. It is calculated as:

\[
\boxed{\text{CCC} = \text{DSO} + \text{DIO} - \text{DPO}}
\]

Where:

- **DSO** = Days Sales Outstanding  
- **DIO** = Days Inventory Outstanding  
- **DPO** = Days Payables Outstanding  

---

### 1. Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)

DSO measures how many days it takes a company to collect payment from customers after a sale.

\[
\text{DSO} = \frac{\text{Average Accounts Receivable}}{\text{Total Credit Sales}} \times \text{Number of Days}
\]

- Higher DSO = slower cash collection.

---

### 2. Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)

DIO measures how many days, on average, inventory sits before it is sold.

\[
\text{DIO} = \frac{\text{Average Inventory}}{\text{Cost of Goods Sold}} \times \text{Number of days}
\]

- Higher DIO means cash is tied up in inventory longer.

---

### 3. Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)

DPO measures how many days a company takes to pay its suppliers.

\[
\text{DPO} = \frac{\text{Average Accounts Payable}}{\text{Cost of Goods Sold}} \times \text{Number of days}
\]

- Higher DPO means the company holds onto its cash longer before paying suppliers.

---

### Why the formula works

- **DSO + DIO** = total days cash is tied up from buying/producing inventory to collecting cash from customers.
- **DPO** is subtracted because the company uses supplier credit to finance part of that time.

So:

\[
\text{CCC} = \text{Time to sell inventory} + \text{Time to collect cash} - \text{Time to pay suppliers}
\]

---

### Example

If a company has:

- DSO = 40 days  
- DIO = 50 days  
- DPO = 30 days  

Then:

\[
\text{CCC} = 40 + 50 - 30 = 60 \text{ days}
\]

This means the company’s cash is tied up for **60 days** between paying for inventory and collecting cash from customers.

---

### Interpretation

- **Lower CCC** is generally better because it means the company converts its investments into cash more quickly.
- **Negative CCC** means the company receives cash from customers before it has to pay its suppliers, which is a strong working capital position.

Credit Default Swaps (CDS) and traditional insurance both transfer credit/default risk, but they are fundamentally different in legal structure, purpose, and regulation.

### 1. Insurable Interest

**Traditional Insurance:**
- Requires the policyholder to have an **insurable interest** in the insured person, property, or liability.
- You cannot buy a fire insurance policy on your neighbor’s house because you would not suffer a direct financial loss if it burned down.
- The purpose is **indemnity**: to make the policyholder whole for an actual loss, not to profit from a loss.

**Credit Default Swaps:**
- Do **not** require an insurable interest.
- A CDS buyer can purchase protection on a bond or loan they do not own. This is called a **“naked” CDS**.
- The buyer is not required to suffer any actual loss from the default; the CDS simply pays out if a specified credit event occurs.
- This allows CDS to be used for **speculation** or **hedging** by parties with no underlying exposure.

### 2. Regulatory Oversight

**Traditional Insurance:**
- Heavily regulated at the **state level** in the U.S. (and by national regulators in most countries).
- Regulators oversee:
  - **Solvency and reserves** – insurers must hold sufficient reserves to pay claims.
  - **Policy forms and rates** – often approved before sale.
  - **Consumer protections** – unfair claims practices, disclosure requirements, and guaranty funds.
  - **Investment restrictions** – insurers face limits on risky investments.
- The focus is on **policyholder protection** and financial stability.

**CDS:**
- Regulated as **derivatives**, not insurance.
- Historically, CDS were largely **unregulated** over-the-counter (OTC) instruments.
- After the 2008 financial crisis, reforms under **Dodd-Frank** (U.S.) and **EMIR** (EU) introduced:
  - **Central clearing** for standardized CDS.
  - **Margin and collateral requirements**.
  - **Trade reporting** to trade repositories.
  - **Capital requirements** for dealers.
- However, CDS regulation focuses on **systemic risk and market transparency**, not consumer protection or insurable interest.
- There is no requirement that a CDS buyer have a loss exposure, and no insurance guaranty fund backs CDS payments.

### Summary

| Feature | Traditional Insurance | Credit Default Swap |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Insurable interest | Required | Not required |
| Purpose | Indemnify actual loss | Hedge or speculate on credit risk |
| Regulatory focus | Consumer protection, solvency, policy terms | Market stability, clearing, margin, transparency |
| Regulator | Insurance regulators | Financial/derivatives regulators (e.g., CFTC, SEC, ESMA) |

In short, CDS are **financial derivatives**, not insurance contracts, and they are regulated as such. The lack of an insurable interest requirement is a key distinction that allows CDS to be used for speculation, while traditional insurance is strictly tied to actual loss exposure.

It identifies adverse selection as occurring before the transaction due to hidden characteristics, and moral hazard as occurring after due to hidden actions. case_results.model_output:
The key difference comes down to **when** the information gap occurs and **what kind** of information is hidden.

| | **Adverse Selection** | **Moral Hazard** |
|---|---|---|
| **When it happens** | Before the contract/transaction | After the contract/transaction |
| **Hidden information** | Hidden **characteristics** or **type** | Hidden **actions** or **behavior** |
| **Core problem** | Bad risks are more likely to select into the deal | Once protected, people take more risk or less care |
| **Common phrase** | “The lemons problem” | “The problem of insurance changing behavior” |

---

### Adverse Selection

Adverse selection occurs when one party has **private information about their own risk or quality** *before* entering into an agreement. The uninformed party cannot tell the “good” types from the “bad” types, so the market tends to attract the bad types.

**Example: Health insurance**  
If insurance companies charge the same premium to everyone, healthy people may decide it’s not worth it and drop out. Sick people, who know they will need expensive care, are more likely to buy insurance. As the pool becomes sicker, premiums rise, driving out more healthy people. The insurer ends up with a pool of high-risk customers — adverse selection.

**Example: Used cars**  
A seller knows if their car is a lemon; the buyer does not. If buyers assume the average car is of medium quality, sellers of lemons are happy to sell, while sellers of good cars may leave the market. Over time, the market fills with lemons.

---

### Moral Hazard
Moral hazard happens when one party is **protected from risk** and therefore has an incentive to behave differently than they would if they bore the full consequences. It occurs **after** the agreement is made, and the hidden element is **action/effort**, not type.

**Example: Insurance**  
Once a person has fire insurance, they may be less careful about smoke detectors or leaving candles lit. Once someone has car insurance, they may drive more recklessly. The insurer cannot easily observe or monitor this behavior, so the insured person takes more risk because the cost of that risk is shifted to the insurer.

**Example: Bank bailouts**  
If a bank knows the government will rescue it if it fails, it may take excessive risks with depositors’ money. The risky behavior happens after the implicit guarantee is in place.

---

### Key Difference in One Sentence

- **Adverse selection** = hidden **information** *before* the deal → bad types are selected.
- **Moral hazard** = hidden **behavior** *after* the deal → people take more risk because they don’t bear the full consequences.

---

### Common Solutions

| Problem | Solutions |
|---|---|
| Adverse selection | Screening, signaling, mandatory insurance, risk-based pricing, warranties |
| Moral hazard | Deductibles, co-payments, monitoring, performance-based pay, collateral |

case_results.model_output:
David Ricardo’s **Law of Comparative Advantage** is one of the most important ideas in economics. It explains why countries can gain from trade even when one country is better at producing *everything*.

## Absolute vs. Comparative Advantage

- **Absolute advantage** means a country can produce a good using fewer resources than another country.
- **Comparative advantage** means a country can produce a good at a **lower opportunity cost** than another country.

The key insight: **What matters for trade is not absolute advantage, but comparative advantage.**

Even if Country A is more efficient at producing both goods, it still cannot be more efficient at producing *everything* relative to itself. Producing more of one good means giving up some of the other. That trade-off — the opportunity cost — is what determines who should produce what.

---

## A Simple Example

Suppose two countries, **England** and **Portugal**, each produce **cloth** and **wine**. Assume they have the same amount of labor, and the labor required per unit is:

| Country | Cloth (hours per unit) | Wine (hours per unit) |
|---|---|---|
| England | 10 | 20 |
| Portugal | 5 | 10 |

Here, Portugal has an **absolute advantage** in both goods: it takes fewer hours to produce both cloth and wine.

But let’s calculate opportunity costs:

- **England**:
  - To produce 1 cloth, it gives up 0.5 wine (10/20).
  - To produce 1 wine, it gives up 2 cloth (20/10).

- **Portugal**:
  - To produce 1 cloth, it gives up 0.5 wine (5/10).
  - To produce 1 wine, it gives up 2 cloth (10/5).

Wait — in this example, the opportunity costs are the same, so there is no comparative advantage. Let’s change the numbers to make the point clearer.

---

## Better Example

| Country | Cloth (hours per unit) | Wine (hours per unit) |
|---|---|---|
| England | 10 | 20 |
| Portugal | 5 | 15 |

Now Portugal is absolutely better at both: it takes fewer hours to produce cloth and wine.

Opportunity costs:

- **England**:
  - 1 cloth = 0.5 wine
  - 1 wine = 2 cloth

- **Portugal**:
  - 1 cloth = 0.33 wine (5/15)
  - 1 wine = 3 cloth (15/5)

So:

- Portugal has a **comparative advantage in cloth** because it gives up only 0.33 wine per cloth, while England gives up 0.5 wine.
- England has a **comparative advantage in wine** because it gives up only 2 cloth per wine, while Portugal gives up 3 cloth.

Even though Portugal is better at both goods, it is **relatively better at cloth**, while England is **relatively less bad at wine**.

---

## Why Trade Benefits Both

If each country specializes in what it has a comparative advantage in:

- Portugal produces cloth.
- England produces wine.

Then they trade. Both can consume more than they could without trade.

For example, suppose Portugal uses 150 hours to produce 30 cloth. England uses 200 hours to produce 10 wine. They trade 1 wine for 2.5 cloth.

- Portugal gets wine at a cost of 2.5 cloth, but if it made wine itself, it would give up 3 cloth per wine. So Portugal gains.
- England gets cloth at a cost of 0.4 wine per cloth, but if it made cloth itself, it would give up 0.5 wine per cloth. So England gains.

Both are better off.

---

## The Core Reason

The reason countries benefit from free trade even when one country has an absolute advantage in everything is:

> **Comparative advantage is based on opportunity cost, not absolute productivity.**

A country can be less efficient in both goods, but it still has a lower opportunity cost in one of them. By specializing in that good and trading, it can get the other good more cheaply than if it produced it itself. The same is true for the more efficient country: it should focus on the good where its advantage is largest.

Thus, **free trade allows countries to specialize, produce more efficiently, and consume more than they could in isolation.**

case_results.model_output:
**Macaulay Duration** is a measure of a bond’s average time to receive its cash flows, weighted by the present value of each cash flow. It is expressed in years.

### Formula

\[
\text{Macaulay Duration} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{t \cdot C_t}{(1+y)^t}}{\sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1+y)^t}}
\]

Where:

- \(t\) = time period until cash flow
- \(C_t\) = cash flow at time \(t\) (coupon or principal)
- \(y\) = yield to maturity per period
- \(n\) = number of periods

The denominator is simply the bond’s current price.

So Macaulay duration is a **weighted average maturity** of the bond’s cash flows, where the weights are the present values of each cash flow.

---

### How It Measures Interest Rate Price Sensitivity

Macaulay Duration itself does not directly give the percentage price change, but it is the foundation for **Modified Duration**, which does.

For a bond with yield \(y\) and coupon frequency \(m\):

\[
\text{Modified Duration} = \frac{\text{Macaulay Duration}}{1 + \frac{y}{m}}
\]

Then the approximate percentage change in bond price for a small change in yield is:

\[
\%\Delta P \approx -\text{Modified Duration} \times \Delta y
\]

So:

- **Higher duration** → greater sensitivity to interest rate changes.
- **Lower duration** → less sensitivity.

For example, if a bond has a Modified Duration of 5, a 1% increase in yield would cause approximately a **5% decrease** in price:

\[
\Delta P \approx -5 \times 0.01 = -0.05 = -5\%
\]

---

### Intuition

Macaulay Duration captures the **timing** of cash flows:

- A zero-coupon bond has Macaulay Duration equal to its maturity, because there is only one cash flow at maturity.
- A coupon bond has a shorter duration than its maturity, because some cash flows arrive earlier.

The longer you must wait to receive your money, the more exposed you are to changes in interest rates — hence higher duration means higher interest rate risk.

---

### Important Caveat

Duration is only a **linear approximation**. For large interest rate changes, bond prices also exhibit **convexity**, so the actual price change is better estimated by:

\[
\Delta P \approx -\text{Modified Duration} \times \Delta y + \frac{1}{2} \times \text{Convexity} \times (\Delta y)^2
\]

But Macaulay Duration remains one of the most important concepts in fixed income for measuring interest rate risk.

A **currency carry trade** is a strategy where an investor borrows money in a currency with a low interest rate and invests it in a currency with a higher interest rate, aiming to profit from the interest rate differential (the “carry”).

### How it works:
1. Borrow in a low-yielding currency (e.g., Japanese yen or Swiss franc).
2. Convert those funds into a high-yielding currency (e.g., Australian dollar, Mexican peso, or Brazilian real).
3. Invest in assets denominated in that high-yielding currency, such as government bonds or money-market instruments.
4. Earn the higher interest rate, and repay the cheaper loan later, hoping the exchange rate stays stable or moves in your favor.

### Primary risk:
The main risk is **exchange rate risk** — specifically, an adverse movement in the currency pair. If the high-yielding currency depreciates against the funding currency, the investor’s profits from the interest-rate differential can be wiped out, and they may suffer significant losses.

This risk is especially severe during “risk-off” events, when investors flee to safe-haven currencies, causing high-yield currencies to fall sharply and low-yield currencies to appreciate — a phenomenon known as **carry trade unwinding**.

case_results.model_output:
Quantitative easing (QE) is a monetary policy tool used by central banks when short-term interest rates are already near zero. It works by expanding the central bank’s balance sheet to push down longer-term interest rates.

Here’s the step-by-step mechanism:

### 1. The central bank creates new reserves
To buy assets, the central bank doesn’t need to borrow or use existing funds. It simply credits the accounts of commercial banks with new reserves. These reserves are a liability on the central bank’s balance sheet.

### 2. The central bank buys long-term securities
The central bank uses those newly created reserves to purchase long-term government bonds (and sometimes mortgage-backed securities) from banks, pension funds, insurance companies, or other financial institutions.

### 3. The balance sheet expands
- **Assets side:** The central bank’s holdings of long-term securities increase.
- **Liabilities side:** The reserves it credits to banks increase by the same amount.

So QE is essentially an asset swap: the private sector gives up long-term bonds and receives bank reserves (a very short-term, safe asset) in return.

### 4. Bond prices rise, long-term yields fall
Because the central bank is a huge buyer of long-term bonds, demand for those bonds increases. Higher demand pushes bond prices up. Since bond yields move inversely to prices, long-term interest rates fall.

### 5. Portfolio rebalancing amplifies the effect
The sellers of the bonds—banks, funds, investors—now hold more reserves or cash than they want. To earn a return, they typically reinvest that money into other assets: corporate bonds, equities, or longer-dated securities. This additional demand pushes up the prices of those assets too, lowering their yields and easing financial conditions more broadly.

### 6. Expectations and signaling
QE also signals that the central bank intends to keep policy loose for a long time. This reduces expectations of future short-term rates, which also helps lower long-term yields.

### In short:
QE expands the central bank’s balance sheet by **buying long-term securities with newly created reserves**. That buying raises bond prices, which lowers long-term yields, and the resulting portfolio rebalancing spreads the easing effect through the wider financial system.

case_results.model_output:
The Internal Rate of Return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes the Net Present Value (NPV) of a project equal to zero:

\[
NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{C_t}{(1+IRR)^t} = 0
\]

For **conventional cash flows** — one initial outflow followed by inflows — the NPV curve crosses the x-axis only once, so there is a single IRR. But for **non-conventional cash flows**, where cash flows change signs more than once (e.g., negative → positive → negative), IRR can produce **multiple solutions** or **misleading results**.

## 1. Multiple IRRs

The NPV equation is a polynomial in \((1+r)^{-t}\). If cash flows change sign more than once, the polynomial can cross zero more than once. For example:

\[
C_0 = -100,\quad C_1 = 230,\quad C_2 = -132
\]

This project has two IRRs: approximately **10%** and **20%**. Both make NPV = 0. Which one is the “true” return? There is no clear answer.

NPV does not have this problem. For a given discount rate, NPV is a single, unambiguous number.

## 2. Misleading reinvestment assumption

IRR implicitly assumes that all intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself. That is often unrealistic, especially if the IRR is very high. NPV assumes cash flows are reinvested at the project’s cost of capital, which is more realistic and consistent with market conditions.

## 3. Misleading for mutually exclusive projects

When comparing two projects, the one with the higher IRR may not have the higher NPV. This happens because IRR ignores:

- **Scale**: A small project with a high IRR may add less value than a large project with a lower IRR.
- **Timing**: A project with earlier cash flows may have a higher IRR, but a project with later cash flows may have a higher NPV at the required return.

NPV directly measures the increase in firm value, so it is generally the better decision rule.

## 4. No unique “rate of return” meaning

For non-conventional cash flows, the IRR is not a meaningful “rate of return” because the project is not simply borrowing money and then paying it back. It may involve multiple periods of financing and investing, so a single discount rate cannot capture the true economic return.

---

### Summary

| Issue | IRR | NPV |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple sign changes | Can produce multiple IRRs | Always one NPV |
| Reinvestment assumption | Assumes reinvestment at IRR | Assumes reinvestment at cost of capital |
| Project scale/timing | Can rank projects incorrectly | Correctly measures value added |
| Decision rule | Ambiguous when multiple IRRs | Clear: accept if NPV > 0 |

So, for non-conventional cash flows, **NPV is the safer and more reliable method** because it avoids multiple solutions and does not rely on unrealistic reinvestment assumptions.

The Dupire local volatility formula is

\[
\boxed{
\sigma_L(K,T)^2
=
\frac{
\displaystyle \frac{\partial C}{\partial T}
+ (r-q)K \frac{\partial C}{\partial K}
+ q\,C(K,T)
}{
\displaystyle \frac12 K^2 \frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial K^2}
}
}
\]

where:

- \(C(K,T)\) is the European call price with strike \(K\) and maturity \(T\),
- \(r\) is the risk-free rate,
- \(q\) is the dividend yield,
- \(\sigma_L(K,T)\) is the local volatility at level \(K\) and time \(T\).

If \(r\) and \(q\) are time-dependent, they are replaced by \(r(T)\) and \(q(T)\).

---

### Why it guarantees perfect calibration to observed implied volatility smiles

European call prices are determined by the risk-neutral density of the underlying asset at maturity:

\[
C(K,T)=e^{-rT}\int_K^\infty (S_T-K)\,f(S_T)\,dS_T.
\]

Differentiating twice with respect to strike gives

\[
\frac{\partial^2 C}{\partial K^2}=e^{-rT} f(K),
\]

so the second strike derivative is proportional to the risk-neutral density of \(S_T\) at \(S_T=K\).

The local volatility model assumes the underlying follows

\[
dS_t = (r-q)S_t\,dt + \sigma_L(S_t,t)\,S_t\,dW_t.
\]

The probability density of \(S_t\) then satisfies the Fokker–Planck forward equation. Dupire’s key insight was to invert this relationship: instead of computing option prices from a given local volatility, one can compute the local volatility directly from the observed option price surface.

The formula above is obtained by substituting the Fokker–Planck equation into the time derivative of the call price and solving for \(\sigma_L^2\). Therefore, by construction, the local volatility surface \(\sigma_L(K,T)\) is exactly the diffusion coefficient that makes the model’s risk-neutral density match the market-implied density for every strike and maturity.

Since European option prices are simply integrals of those densities, the local volatility model reproduces all observed European call prices, and hence all implied volatility smiles, exactly. This is why Dupire’s formula is said to guarantee perfect calibration to the observed implied volatility surface, provided the market prices are smooth and arbitrage-free.

Here is a contrast between Utilitarianism and Deontological Ethics, focusing on their core principles and key differences.

---

### 1. Utilitarianism (Jeremy Bentham & John Stuart Mill)

**Core Principle:** The morality of an action is determined by its consequences. The best action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people. This is called the **Principle of Utility**.

- **Jeremy Bentham (Classical Utilitarianism):** Bentham was a hedonist—he believed pleasure and pain are the only things that matter. He created a "hedonic calculus" to measure the amount of pleasure an action produces based on intensity, duration, certainty, etc. For Bentham, all pleasures are equal; pushpin is as good as poetry if it produces the same amount of pleasure.
- **John Stuart Mill (Refined Utilitarianism):** Mill argued that not all pleasures are equal. He distinguished between **higher pleasures** (intellectual, moral, aesthetic) and **lower pleasures** (physical, sensory). He famously said, "It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied." Mill also introduced the idea of **rule utilitarianism**—we should follow rules that generally promote happiness, even if a specific act might not.

**Key Features:**
- **Consequentialist:** The ends justify the means.
- **Focus on the collective:** The happiness of the group outweighs the happiness of the individual.
- **Empirical and pragmatic:** It requires calculating outcomes and predicting consequences.
- **Moral flexibility:** An action can be right in one situation and wrong in another, depending on the outcome.

---

### 2. Deontological Ethics (Immanuel Kant)

**Core Principle:** The morality of an action is based on whether it follows a universal moral duty, regardless of the consequences. For Kant, the only thing that is good without qualification is a **good will**—the intention to do one's duty.

Kant's ethics is built on the **Categorical Imperative**, which has several formulations:

1. **Universal Law:** "Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law." If you cannot rationally will that everyone act the same way, then the action is wrong.
2. **Humanity Formula:** "Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end and never merely as a means to an end." People are not tools to be used for other people's happiness.
3. **Kingdom of Ends:** Act as if you were a legislator in a kingdom of ends, where everyone is both a ruler and a subject.

### Key Features:
- **Non-consequentialist:** The outcome does not matter; the intention and the rule do.
- **Focus on the individual:** Every person has inherent dignity and worth, and cannot be sacrificed for the collective good.
- **Rational and universal:** Moral laws are discovered through reason and apply to all rational beings at all times.
- **Rigid:** If an action is wrong (e.g., lying), it is always wrong, even if it produces a good outcome.

---

### Direct Contrast

| Feature | Utilitarianism (Bentham/Mill) | Deontology (Kant) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Question** | "What will happen?" | "What is my duty?" |
| **Basis of Morality** | Consequences (outcomes) | Duty and intention (motives) |
| **Goal** | Maximize happiness / minimize suffering | Respect rational nature and universal law |
| **View of the Individual** | One unit in the collective | An end in itself, never a means |
| **Flexibility** | Flexible; rules can be broken if it helps | Rigid; rules are absolute and universal |
| **Decision-Making** | Empirical calculation of pleasure/pain | Rational deduction of universal maxims |
| **Example: Lying** | Wrong if it causes more harm than good; right if it saves a life | Always wrong, because a universal law of lying would destroy trust and communication |
| **Example: Punishing an innocent person** | Justified if it prevents a riot and brings peace to the majority | Never justified, because it treats the innocent person as a mere means to an end |

---

## Classic Example: The Lying to a Murderer

Imagine a murderer comes to your door asking for the location of your friend, who is hiding inside.

- **Utilitarian (Mill):** You should lie. The lie produces a good outcome (saving a life) and prevents the murderer from causing harm. The happiness of the friend and the murderer's potential victim outweighs the minor harm of lying.
- **Deontologist (Kant):** You must not lie. Lying is a violation of the categorical imperative. If everyone lied, trust would be destroyed, and the concept of truth would collapse. You are responsible for your own moral duty, not for the murderer's actions. (Kant famously argued that you should tell the truth, even if it leads to a bad outcome, because you cannot control the consequences, only your own will.)

---

### Criticisms

- **Utilitarianism:** Critics argue it can justify terrible acts (e.g., sacrificing an innocent person) if the overall happiness is increased. It also requires impossible calculations of future consequences and can be too demanding (we would constantly have to sacrifice our own happiness for others).
- **Deontology:** Critics argue it is too rigid and can lead to morally absurd outcomes (e.g., telling the truth to a murderer). It also fails to provide a clear way to resolve conflicts between duties (e.g., when the duty to tell the truth conflicts with the duty to protect life).

---

### Summary

In short, **Utilitarianism** is a **consequentialist** theory that says "the ends justify the means" if the overall happiness is maximized. **Deontology** is a **duty-based** theory that says "the means must be just, regardless of the ends." Bentham and Mill focus on the **outcome**; Kant focuses on the **intention and the universal moral law**.

Descartes’ proposition **“Cogito, ergo sum”** — usually translated as **“I think, therefore I am”** — is the most famous moment in his *Meditations on First Philosophy*. It is his answer to the question: **Is there anything I can know with absolute certainty?**

### The Context: Methodical Doubt

In the *Meditations*, Descartes sets out to find a firm and lasting foundation for knowledge. To do this, he uses a method of **radical doubt**: he doubts everything that could possibly be doubted, even if the doubt is only hypothetical.

- He doubts the evidence of the senses, because they sometimes deceive us.
- He doubts even mathematical truths, by imagining an **evil demon** who could be deceiving him about everything.
- He doubts the existence of the external world, his body, and even his own memories.

After this sweeping doubt, almost everything seems uncertain. But one thing resists all doubt: **the act of doubting itself**. If he is doubting, he is thinking. And if he is thinking, then there must be something that is doing the thinking.

Thus Descartes arrives at the indubitable truth:

> **Cogito, ergo sum** — I think, therefore I am.

### What the Cogito Means

The *cogito* is not meant as a logical syllogism like:

- Whatever thinks exists.
- I think.
- Therefore I exist.

Descartes insists it is known **immediately and intuitively**, not by deduction. In the very act of thinking, I directly grasp my own existence. Even if an evil demon is deceiving me, the fact that I am being deceived means I exist. As Descartes puts it in the *Meditations*:

> “I am, I exist” is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.

So the *cogito* is a **performative certainty**: the very attempt to doubt it proves it true.

### Its Role as a Foundational Truth

The *cogito* is Descartes’ **Archimedean point** — a fixed, certain truth on which he can build the rest of knowledge.

From this foundation, Descartes derives:

1. **The nature of the self**: I am a “thinking thing” (*res cogitans*) — a being whose essence is thought, not body.
2. **The criterion of truth**: Whatever I perceive **clearly and distinctly** is true. The *cogito* is the first clear and distinct idea.
3. **The existence of God**: Descartes argues that the idea of God is clear and distinct, and that only God could be its cause. God’s existence guarantees that our clear and distinct perceptions are reliable.
4. **The external world**: Once God is known to be no deceiver, Descartes argues that our senses can be trusted, and the material world exists.

In this way, the *cogito* is not just a clever phrase — it is the **first brick** in Descartes’s project to overcome skepticism and establish a secure foundation for science and philosophy.

### In Short

**“Cogito, ergo sum”** means that the one thing I cannot doubt is my own existence, because the very act of doubting or thinking proves it. In the *Meditations*, it serves as the foundational truth from which Descartes attempts to rebuild all knowledge — the certainty that stands even in the face of radical doubt.

Ferdinand de Saussure, the Swiss linguist often called the father of modern linguistics and semiotics, introduced a foundational model of the **linguistic sign** in his *Course in General Linguistics* (1916). For Saussure, the sign is not simply a word that points to a thing in the world; rather, it is a **two-sided psychological entity** that unites a concept and a sound-image.

Saussure defines the sign as composed of two inseparable parts:

### 1. The Signifier (*signifiant*)
- This is the **form** of the sign: the “sound-image” or the physical/psychological shape of a word as we hear or say it.
- It is not the actual physical sound itself, but the **mental impression** of that sound — the way the word exists in our mind.
- For example, the spoken or mental sequence of sounds “t-r-e-e” is the signifier.

### 2. The Signified (*signifié*)
- This is the **concept** or **meaning** that the signifier refers to.
- It is not the actual physical object in the world, but the **mental concept** of that object.
- For example, the idea of a tree — its general image, characteristics, and meaning — is the signified.

### The Sign as a Whole
For Saussure, the sign is the **combination** of the signifier and the signified:

> **Sign = Signifier + Signified**

He compared the sign to a sheet of paper: you cannot cut the front without also cutting the back. Similarly, the signifier and signified are inseparable; one has no meaning without the other.

### Key Principles

- **Arbitrariness of the sign:** The relationship between the signifier and the signified is arbitrary. There is no natural or necessary connection between the sound-image “tree” and the concept of a tree. This is why different languages use different signifiers for the same concept: *tree*, *arbre*, *Baum*, *árbol*.

- **The sign is relational and differential**: A sign has meaning not in isolation, but through its differences from other signs. For example, “cat” means what it does partly because it is not “cap,” “bat,” or “cut.”

- **No direct reference to reality**: Saussure’s sign does not directly connect a word to an object in the external world. Instead, it connects a sound-image to a concept. The actual object is called the **referent**, which lies outside Saussure’s model of the sign.

### Summary
In Saussurean semiotics, the sign is a two-sided mental entity:

- **Signifier** = the form (sound-image)
- **Signified** = the concept (meaning)

Together, they produce **signification** — the act of meaning-making. This model became the foundation of structuralism and modern semiotics, showing that language is not a naming system but a system of signs based on convention, difference, and structure.

Here is a comparison of Thomas Hobbes’ and John Locke’s views of the State of Nature, focusing on their respective works *Leviathan* and the *Second Treatise of Government*.

---

### 1. The State of Nature as a Starting Point

Both Hobbes and Locke use the “state of nature” as a hypothetical or historical condition to explain why political authority is necessary. But they describe it in radically different ways.

- **Hobbes** (*Leviathan*, 1651): The state of nature is a **state of war**. Because all humans are roughly equal in body and mind, and because resources are scarce, everyone has a right to everything, including another person’s body. This leads to a “war of all against all” in which life is famously:
  > “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.”

- **Locke** (*Second Treatise of Government*, 1689): The state of nature is a state of **peace, liberty, and equality**, but it is not a state of license. It is governed by the **law of nature**, which is reason. In this state, no one has more power than anyone else, and all are free to act as they wish—provided they do not harm others in their life, health, liberty, or possessions.

---

## 2. Human Nature and Equality

- **Hobbes** sees humans as driven by **self-preservation, competition, diffidence (distrust), and glory**. Equality is a problem: because people are roughly equal, they can all hope to dominate others, which leads to conflict. There is no natural moral order in the state of nature; justice and injustice do not exist until a sovereign is created.

- **Locke** also sees humans as equal, but for him equality is a moral principle: because all are made by God and share the same nature, no one is naturally subordinate to another. Humans are rational and capable of understanding the natural law. They are not naturally at war; they are naturally social and cooperative, though they may be tempted to violate the law when their own interests are involved.

---

## 3. Natural Law and Rights

- **Hobbes**: In the state of nature, there is no objective right or wrong. The only “right” is the **right of nature** – the liberty each person has to do whatever is necessary to preserve their own life. Since everyone has this right to everything, it is effectively a right to nothing. There is no property, no justice, no injustice. The only natural law is a **prudential rule of reason**: seek peace, and if you cannot get peace, use all advantages of war.

- **Locke**: The state of nature is governed by a **binding natural law** that is discoverable by reason. This law says:
  - No one may harm another in his life, health, liberty, or possessions.
  - Everyone has a right to punish those who violate the law, because in the state of nature everyone is an executive of the law of nature.
  - Property is acquired through labor: by mixing one’s labor with the common resources of nature, a person makes it his own, provided enough and as good is left for others.

---

## 4. The Problem with the State of Nature

- **Hobbes**: The state of nature is so terrible that the only solution is to escape it at any cost. The problem is **constant fear and insecurity**. Without a common power, there is no law, no property, no industry, no culture, no society. The only solution is to create an **absolute sovereign** – a Leviathan – by a social contract in which everyone gives up their rights to a single ruler or assembly.

- **Locke**: The state of nature is not a state of war, but it is **inconvenient**. The problems are:
  1. There is no established, settled, known law.
  2. There is no impartial judge to settle disputes.
  3. There is no power to enforce the law.
  
  These inconveniences make it rational to form a civil society, but the purpose is to **protect** natural rights, not to escape a war of all against all.

---

## 5. The Social Contract and Government

- **Hobbes**: The social contract is a **transfer of rights** to a sovereign. The sovereign is not a party to the contract, so he cannot be accused of breaking it. The sovereign’s power is **absolute and indivisible**. Subjects have no right to rebel, because rebellion would return them to the state of nature, which is worse. Even a bad sovereign is better than the state of nature.

- **Locke**: The social contract is a **trust**. People consent to form a community and then establish a government to protect their natural rights. The government is **limited** and must rule by consent. If the government violates the trust – for example, by taking property without consent or by becoming tyrannical – the people have the right to **dissolve the government** and replace it. The state of nature is not so terrible that any tyranny is preferable.

---

## 6. Property

- **Hobbes**: There is no property in the state of nature. Property only exists after the sovereign is established, because the sovereign defines what is “mine” and “yours.” The sovereign’s power over property is absolute.

- **Locke**: Property exists in the state of nature through labor. The purpose of government is to protect property, and government cannot take property without the consent of the people. This is a major difference: for Locke, property is a natural right; for Hobbes, it is a creation of the state.

---

## 7. Key Differences in a Nutshell

| | Hobbes | Locke |
|---|---|---|
| State of nature | War of all against all | Peace, liberty, equality |
| Human nature | Selfish, competitive, fearful | Rational, cooperative, but biased |
| Natural law | None (only prudential rules) | Binding moral law of reason |
| Natural rights | Right to everything (useless) | Life, liberty, property |
| Property | Created by sovereign | Natural right via labor |
| Government | Absolute, indivisible | Limited, by consent |
| Revolution | Never justified | Justified if government violates trust |

---

## Conclusion

Hobbes and Locke both use the state of nature to justify political authority, but they reach opposite conclusions. Hobbes sees the state of nature as a nightmare of insecurity, so he argues for an absolute sovereign to impose order. Locke sees it as a tolerable but inconvenient condition, so he argues for a limited government that protects natural rights and can be overthrown if it fails. Their different views of human nature and natural law lead directly to their different theories of government: one authoritarian, one liberal.
